title: Benchmarking Sensor-Fault Robustness in Forecasting
claim: A benchmark is specified by its task scope, a suite of controlled fault scenarios, a sampling-to-score protocol, and aggregated comparison axes.
layout: 4 panels A–D, left-to-right with D under C, rounded cards
description: A four-panel benchmark overview. Panel A, on the left, lists four forecasting datasets (Beijing Air, Penmanshiel WT08, ETTh1, Traffic). Each has small blue bars for input channels and forecast targets and green bars for input window and horizon. Panel B, in the center, is the largest. It shows eight mini time-series plots with a black clean signal and a red faulty one, grouped as Value (drift, attenuation, noise, spike), Timing (time stretch, compress) and Availability (stuck sensor, missing data). Below them, low-severity and high-severity channel-by-time grids use pink-to-red shading to show fault intensity on the input history X while the target Y stays clean. Panel C, top right, shows a three-box flow (sample data, sample severity, evaluate model) above the three metric formulas. Panel D, bottom right, shows dataset × architecture × method axes, a heatmap and a Pareto-style scatter.
caption: Benchmark overview for SensorFault-Bench. The benchmark perturbs observed input histories while keeping forecast targets fixed. The scored set P contains eight value, timing, and availability scenarios over one severity axis. Evaluation estimates degradation per scenario and reports worst-scenario degradation with clean MSE and worst-scenario fault-time MSE. Panels A–C show task scope, scenario suite, and sampling-to-score flow. Panel D compares clean error with degradation after aggregating results across datasets, architectures, robustness-improvement methods, and scenarios.
abstract: Cyber-physical system (CPS) forecasting models depend on sensor streams with noisy, biased, missing, or temporally misaligned readings, yet standard forecasting evaluation often selects models by nominal error without showing whether they remain robust under such faults. We introduce SensorFault-Bench, a CPS-grounded protocol that evaluates forecasting architectures and robustness-improvement methods through controlled synthetic stress tests of isolated input faults, together with an operational taxonomy of the methods. Across four real-world datasets and eight scored scenarios governed by a standardized severity model, it reports worst-scenario degradation, clean mean squared error (MSE), and worst-scenario fault-time MSE, separating relative robustness from absolute error. Explicit fault-training methods train on adjacent fault families disjoint from the scored scenarios. Empirically, forecasting architectures favored by clean MSE can degrade sharply under faults, and clean-MSE rankings can disagree with worst-scenario fault-time error rankings. Chronos-2, the evaluated zero-shot foundation model, matches or trails the last-value naive forecaster in clean MSE on the two single-target datasets and has the largest worst-scenario degradation on ETTh1 and Traffic, where all channels are forecast targets. For the evaluated robustness-improvement method set, paired deltas show selective degradation reductions: projected gradient descent adversarial training and randomized training lead where value faults dominate observed degradation, and fault augmentation leads on Traffic, where availability faults dominate. High degradation reveals fault sensitivity that clean MSE misses, while low degradation supports robustness only within the evaluated scenarios. The benchmark therefore screens forecasters before use in a specific deployment, which requires validation against its recorded faults.
